SECURITY DEPOSIT & PRORATED RENT CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What's the refund, and what's the prorated rent?

Two calculators for the arithmetic every move-in or move-out raises: itemize a security deposit's deductions to see the refund or balance due, and calculate prorated rent for a partial first or last month. Both run entirely in this browser. The deposit side then copies out as a plain-text itemized statement you can paste into an email — the document a landlord has to send, and the line-by-line math a tenant needs to check one charge rather than argue about a total.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

Security deposit refund

Some states and cities require a landlord to pay interest on a held deposit (for example New York for buildings with six or more units, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Maryland) — check your own jurisdiction and lease. Leave the rate blank if none applies; if one does, enter the rate it sets and this adds the accrued interest to the refund.

Itemized deductions

Enter the deposit amount, add each deduction, and click Calculate refund.

Deposit settlement

Line itemAmount

Copies the deposit, each named deduction, the total, and the refund or balance as plain text to paste into an email or a dispute. The “arithmetic only, not a legal determination” note is copied with it.

Prorated rent

Enter monthly rent, days in the month, and days occupied, then click Calculate.

Prorated rent result

What this does and doesn't do

Both calculators total the numbers you enter — a deposit amount and a list of deductions, or a monthly rent and a day count. Neither one knows your state's itemized-statement deadline, deposit limit, interest rules, or what specifically counts as normal wear and tear versus damage in your jurisdiction. Treat the output as the arithmetic behind your own itemization or dispute, not a legal determination.

Already using a property-management platform like TurboTenant for listings and rent collection? See how this differs for the one-off arithmetic of settling a single deposit or prorating a single partial month.

Tracking the deduction in a spreadsheet instead? See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet for what a plain subtraction misses — an unlabeled deduction, a prorated-interest formula, and a copy-ready statement that can't drift from the numbers on screen.

Common questions

How do you calculate a security deposit refund?

Add up every itemized deduction (unpaid rent, cleaning, repairs, or other charges) and subtract the total from the deposit amount. If the deductions are less than the deposit, the difference is the refund due. If deductions exceed the deposit, the difference is a balance owed instead.

What is prorated rent and how is it calculated?

Prorated rent covers a partial month, usually the first or last month of a lease. It is calculated as a daily rate (monthly rent divided by the number of days in that month) multiplied by the number of days actually occupied.

Can a landlord deduct for normal wear and tear?

Most landlord-tenant frameworks distinguish normal wear and tear (ordinary aging from everyday use, generally not deductible) from actual damage beyond normal use (generally deductible) — but the exact definition, itemization deadline, and any deposit limits vary by state and by the lease itself. Check your local law and lease before finalizing a number.

Does this calculator include interest on the deposit?

Only if you enter a rate. Some states and cities require a landlord to pay interest on a held deposit (for example New York for buildings with six or more units, Massachusetts, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Maryland), at a rate the jurisdiction sets and that changes over time. This calculator does not know whether your jurisdiction requires it or what the current rate is — enter the rate that applies to you and how many days the deposit was held, and it adds the accrued interest to the refund. Leave the rate blank if none applies.

Can I copy the itemization out to send to the other party?

Yes. After you calculate the refund, “Copy itemized statement” puts the deposit, every named deduction and its amount, the total, and the refund or balance owed on your clipboard as plain text — ready to paste into an email, a letter, or a message. It is the same arithmetic shown on this page, so the copy can never disagree with the table. The note saying this is arithmetic and not a legal determination of what may be deducted is copied along with it, because the person receiving the statement never sees this page. If your browser blocks clipboard access, the statement appears in a text box you can select and copy instead.

Is this legal advice?

No. This calculator only totals the numbers you enter — it does not determine what is legally deductible, does not know your state's rules or deadlines, and is not a substitute for reviewing your lease or consulting a qualified professional.

normal-wear-and-tear-vs-damage.html.text:
← Security Deposit Refund & Prorated Rent Calculator

Normal wear and tear vs. damage: how to itemize a deposit deduction

Most security deposit disputes come down to one question: is this ordinary wear and tear the rent already paid for, or damage beyond normal use? The line is not a formula, but it is consistent enough to itemize deductions that hold up rather than get disputed line by line.

Open the free deposit refund calculator

The dividing line

Normal wear and tear is the ordinary decline any surface shows from everyday use over the length of a tenancy: faded paint, a worn path in carpet, small nail holes from hung pictures, a loose door hinge, minor scuffs on a wall. It happens no matter how careful the tenant is, and it is generally treated as a cost of doing business -- something the rent, not the deposit, already covers.

Damage is harm beyond that ordinary use: a hole punched in drywall, a burn or deep stain that ordinary cleaning will not remove, a broken fixture or appliance, a cracked window, or pet damage beyond what a professional cleaning would fix. The practical test most landlord-tenant frameworks apply is whether the condition resulted from ordinary, expected use of the unit as intended, or from negligence, abuse, an accident, or simple neglect.

Side-by-side examples

ConditionUsually wear and tearUsually damage
CarpetWorn traffic paths, flattened pileBurns, unremovable stains, pet-chewed corners
WallsSmall nail holes, minor scuffs, faded paintLarge holes, unrepaired crayon or marker, water damage from neglect
FixturesLoose hinges, worn faucet finishBroken fixtures, missing parts
WindowsHard-water spottingCracked or broken glass, missing screens
CleanlinessLight dust, faint cooking odorTrash left behind, heavy grime, infestation from neglect

These are common patterns, not a legal standard. Any of them can come out differently depending on your lease's own terms and your jurisdiction's rules.

How tenancy length affects the wear-and-tear line

Yes, tenancy length matters, in how a reasonable deduction is judged even where the law does not spell out an exact formula. A five-year tenant's worn carpet is expected wear; the same wear after a five-month lease looks a lot more like damage. Some frameworks explicitly prorate deductions for flooring, paint, or appliances against an expected useful life for exactly this reason -- charging full replacement cost for a ten-year-old carpet nearing the end of its life is a common way a deduction gets successfully disputed. Check whether your jurisdiction or lease requires this kind of proration before charging a full replacement price.

What documentation actually holds up

  • Dated photos or video from move-in and move-out. A move-out photo alone proves the condition existed; it does not prove the tenant caused it. Paired photos do.
  • A signed move-in condition checklist. The single strongest piece of evidence in a deposit dispute, because it establishes the starting point both parties agreed to.
  • An actual repair invoice, or a specific, itemized estimate. "Cleaning: $400" invites a dispute. "Carpet cleaning, 2 bedrooms + hallway, per attached invoice: $180" does not.
  • A line item per deduction, not one lump sum. A single total forces the other party to dispute everything at once to dispute anything; itemized lines let both sides agree on what is not contested and focus only on what is.

Common questions

What is the difference between normal wear and tear and damage?

Normal wear and tear is the ordinary decline every surface shows from everyday use over the length of a tenancy -- faded paint, worn carpet paths, small nail holes, loose door hinges. Damage is harm beyond that ordinary use -- a hole punched in drywall, a burn or stain that ordinary cleaning will not lift, a broken fixture, pet damage beyond a stain a carpet cleaner removes. The practical test most frameworks use is whether the condition resulted from ordinary, expected use of the unit as intended, or from negligence, abuse, or an accident.

Can a landlord deduct for normal wear and tear?

Generally no -- normal wear and tear is treated as a cost of doing business that the rent already covers, not something a deposit is meant to cover. Actual damage beyond normal use is generally deductible. The exact legal definition, any deposit-return deadline, and whether itemization must be in writing all vary by jurisdiction and by the lease itself, so check local law and the lease before finalizing a number.

Does the length of the tenancy matter?

Yes, in how a reasonable deduction is judged even where the law does not spell out a formula. A five-year tenant's worn carpet is expected; the same wear after five months looks more like damage. Some frameworks explicitly prorate flooring, paint, or appliance deductions against an expected useful life for this reason -- check whether yours does before charging full replacement cost.

What documentation actually holds up for a deduction?

Dated photos or video from both move-in and move-out, a signed move-in condition checklist, and the actual repair invoice or a specific, itemized repair estimate -- not a round number with no backup. A deduction line that names the item, the actual or estimated cost, and points to a photo is far harder to dispute than one that just states a total.

Is this legal advice about what I can deduct?

No. This page explains the general distinction landlord-tenant frameworks draw and how to document a deduction so it holds up; it does not state your jurisdiction's specific rules, deadlines, or dollar limits. Check your local law and lease, or a qualified professional, before finalizing what you deduct.

Itemize your deductions in the free calculator

No warranty. This page is not legal, financial, or tax advice, and it does not state any specific jurisdiction's rules, deadlines, or dollar limits. Verify against your local law, your lease, and a qualified professional before finalizing any deduction.

vs-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Security deposit refund & prorated rent calculator

This calculator vs. a spreadsheet

A lot of landlords and tenants already reach for a spreadsheet at move-out: one column for each deduction, a subtotal, a formula that subtracts it from the deposit. That arithmetic is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What it does not do on its own is flag the mistakes that actually cause disputes: an unlabeled deduction, a balance that has quietly gone negative, an interest formula entered once and never rechecked, or a statement that drifted from the sheet because it was retyped into an email by hand.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What's the deposit minus the deductions? Either one — a spreadsheet subtracts fine.
Did I forget to describe one of the deduction line items? This calculator — flags any deduction with no description before you send it.
Do the deductions exceed the deposit — is this a refund or a balance owed? This calculator — labels the result explicitly rather than leaving a negative cell to interpret.
My jurisdiction requires deposit interest. What's the prorated amount? This calculator — enter the rate and days held; a rate with no days (or the reverse) is flagged instead of silently returning zero.
Can I send the other party a statement that can't drift from my own numbers? This calculator — the copy button builds the statement from the settlement already on screen, and disables itself if you edit an input without recalculating.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere? No, on either — but this calculator needs no account, no template, and no formula to maintain.
Calculate a refund or prorated rent now

This tool needs no account and nothing installed: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and the deposit amount, every deduction, and every rent figure you enter stay on this device — nothing is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't a security deposit refund just deposit minus deductions?

The subtraction is trivial and a spreadsheet does it fine. What a plain spreadsheet does not do on its own is flag a deduction with no description, catch the case where deductions exceed the deposit (a balance owed, not a refund), or keep the copy you send the other party from silently drifting away from the number your own sheet shows — because that copy usually gets retyped by hand into an email.

Why is prorating deposit interest harder in a spreadsheet than it looks?

Interest is deposit times the jurisdiction's annual rate times days held over 365, and every deposit calculator or landlord's own sheet has to encode that formula once and then trust it every time a rate or a day count changes. Enter a rate with no day count, or a day count with no rate, and a spreadsheet cell just returns zero with no explanation — this calculator flags that combination explicitly instead of returning a silent zero.

What's actually different about the itemized statement this produces?

The statement is generated from the exact settlement figures already on screen, not retyped from them. Editing a deduction after calculating, without recalculating, disables the copy button rather than handing out a statement that disagrees with the table above it — a spreadsheet-to-email copy has no equivalent safeguard, because the retype is a separate, unchecked step.

Does this replace a landlord's own record-keeping spreadsheet?

No. A spreadsheet or ledger that tracks every tenant, every deposit, and every move-out date over years is still the right tool for that ongoing record. This page answers one settlement at a time — what does this deposit refund to, or what does this partial month prorate to — and nothing it computes is saved anywhere once you leave the page.

This calculator vs. TurboTenant

TurboTenant is a landlord property-management platform: listing a vacancy, screening applicants, signing an e-lease, collecting rent, and, on its paid plans, tracking a security deposit against that lease record. It is a system for running a rental end to end.

This page is not a property-management system and never will be. It answers one narrower question, on the spot: what does this deposit settle to, or what does this partial month prorate to — typed in your browser, with no account, no property record, and nothing saved anywhere.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to list a vacancy, screen an applicant, and get a lease signed. TurboTenant — that's the workflow it's built for.
I want rent collected online every month without chasing a check. TurboTenant — ongoing rent collection is a core feature.
A tenant is moving out. What's the refund once I list the deductions? This calculator — enter the deposit and each deduction, get the number immediately.
The tenant moved in mid-month. What's the prorated rent for that first month? This calculator — enter the monthly rent, days in the month, and days occupied.
I'm a tenant and want to check the landlord's deduction math myself. This calculator — the same free form works from either side of the lease.
Can I see the refund figure without creating a property-management account? This calculator — a static page, no account, nothing uploaded.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or TurboTenant?

They solve different problems, and a landlord who uses TurboTenant for everything else can still land here for one calculation. TurboTenant is a property-management platform: listings, tenant screening, e-signable leases, online rent collection, and (on its paid plans) security deposit tracking held alongside a specific lease record in its own system. This page is a single free form that does none of that. You type a deposit amount and list each deduction, or a monthly rent and a day count, and it does the arithmetic — refund or balance owed, or a prorated partial-month figure — with nothing signed up for and no lease on file anywhere.

Do I need a property-management account just to work out a deposit refund?

No, and that is the gap this page exists to close. A landlord managing one unit, or a tenant checking a landlord's math from the other side of the table, does not need an account, a listed property, or a stored lease to add up deductions against a deposit. This calculator runs the same subtraction TurboTenant's deposit tracking runs, without the account, the property record, or the plan tier deposit tracking sits behind.

Does this replace TurboTenant's property management?

No. Listing a vacancy, screening applicants, signing a lease, and collecting rent every month are real, recurring jobs, and a platform built around a persistent record of the tenancy is the right tool for that. This page sells nothing, stores nothing, and has no concept of a property or a lease term. It answers one arithmetic question — what does this deposit settle to, or what does this partial month prorate to — the same question a landlord who already uses full property-management software still has to answer at move-out.

Is this page affiliated with TurboTenant?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by TurboTenant, and this page is not a review of it. Its plans, pricing, and features change; check TurboTenant's own site for current terms rather than relying on any description here.
